opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's extremely expensive, and the cost isn't just the hardware.

Let's do a rough calculation. A full-size humanoid today, with reasonably good dexterous hands, costs somewhere in the hundreds of thousands of RMB, even at scale. Ten thousand of them is already billions before you collect any data. But the hardware is only the start. Each robot needs a teleoperator, so you're also hiring and training thousands of people and running shifts. You need space and you need scene setups, because if every robot collects data in the same lab, the data has very little diversity. Then there's maintenance. Humanoids break, especially hands and joints under heavy daily use, so a meaningful fraction of the fleet is always down. Add data cleaning, annotation, storage, and quality control. In total, you're looking at an annual operating cost on the order of the hardware cost itself, possibly more.

The deeper question is what you get for that money. Teleoperated real-world data is very high quality, but it scales linearly with people and robot-hours. Even with ten thousand robots running all day, you might get tens of millions of trajectories a year. That sounds like a lot, but compare it with language models trained on trillions of tokens, or vision models trained on billions of images. For a generalizable embodied foundation model, covering all the objects, lighting conditions, environments, and failure cases, that volume is still far from enough. And the data is tied to one hardware generation. When you change the hand or the body design next year, a large part of that dataset loses value.

So my view has always been that real-world teleoperation data is necessary but shouldn't be the main source of scale. The bulk of the data, especially for things like grasping, navigation, and basic manipulation, should come from simulation and synthetic data, where we can generate huge numbers of scenes, objects, and physical variations at a tiny fraction of the cost. Real data is then used precisely: to close the sim-to-real gap, to cover tasks where physics simulation still falls short, like deformable objects or contact-rich assembly, and to post-train and align the model.

You could compare it to a pyramid. At the base is massive synthetic data and internet video, in the middle is a moderate amount of real robot data, and at the top is a small amount of very targeted data from deployment. If you try to build the whole pyramid out of real teleoperation data, the cost explodes and you still won't reach the scale you need.

There's also a practical point. Once robots are actually deployed doing useful work in factories, retail, or pharmacies, they generate data while also creating value. That's a much healthier loop than paying ten thousand robots purely to collect data. So I'd rather spend the money to get the model good enough for deployment, using sim and synthetic data, and let the deployed fleet become the data engine.

r001.rationale: The response mentions teleoperators and running shifts, but does not say that multiple shifts can require four human operators per robot.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when you actually run the numbers, it's a very sobering exercise. People throw around "ten thousand robots" as if it were a software figure, but these are physical machines. A full-size humanoid today, even at relatively optimistic volume pricing, is somewhere in the range of a few hundred thousand yuan. Multiply that by ten thousand and you're already at several billion yuan just for the hardware. And that's before anything has actually happened.

Then comes what I think people consistently underestimate: the hardware is really only the entry ticket. Every one of those robots needs an operator if you're doing teleoperation, and a good teleoperator is not someone you hire off the street. There's a learning curve, there's fatigue, and the data quality varies enormously from person to person. So you're carrying ten thousand salaries, plus training, plus the space to house all of this, plus electricity, plus the networking and storage infrastructure to actually move and store the data. Running costs over a year can easily rival or exceed the upfront hardware spend.

And then there's the part nobody likes to talk about: maintenance. Humanoids at today's maturity level break. Joints wear out, motors overheat, cables fray, sensors drift. If you have ten thousand units and even a small percentage are down at any given time, that's hundreds of machines sitting idle while you still pay for them. The maintenance team itself becomes a significant organization.

So my rough view is that a ten-thousand-robot data factory is really a ten-billion-yuan-scale commitment once you account for everything over two or three years. That's a very serious number, and it only makes sense if you believe the data you get is dramatically better than what you'd get from alternatives.

And that's where I'd push back a bit on the whole premise. The question isn't just "can we afford it," it's "is this the most efficient way to get the data we need." Full-body real-robot teleoperation data is the most expensive form of data there is, per sample. If a large portion of what you need can come from simulation, from human video, from cheaper hand-held devices or data gloves, or from synthetic generation, then you can shrink that real-robot fleet dramatically while still covering the critical gap of real-world physical interaction. I'd rather see a few hundred robots used very deliberately in the places where real data is irreplaceable, than ten thousand robots collecting a lot of redundant demonstrations of the same pick-and-place tasks.

So I'd say the cost is real, it's enormous, and it forces you to be very clear about what the data is actually for. If you can't answer that, ten thousand robots is a very expensive way to find out.

r001.rationale: The response says each teleoperated robot needs an operator and mentions staffing costs, but it does not explain that multiple shifts can require four operators per robot.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the cost of buying the robots from the cost of running a useful data collection operation. At ten thousand full-size humanoids, every additional hundred thousand yuan per robot adds a billion yuan to the hardware bill. And that’s before maintenance, replacement parts, facilities, operators, and the infrastructure to store and process the data.

The more important question is how much useful data you get for that investment. How many hours can each robot operate reliably? How much human intervention does it need? Are those ten thousand robots collecting diverse experiences, or repeating essentially the same task?

So I wouldn’t start by targeting ten thousand robots. I’d first establish, with a smaller fleet, the cost per hour of usable data and whether that data actually improves the model. Once that relationship is clear, you have a basis for deciding whether scaling up makes economic sense.

r001.rationale: The response mentions operators and human intervention as costs, but does not state that multiple teleoperation shifts can require four human operators per robot.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the cost of buying the robots from the cost of collecting useful data. With ten thousand full-size humanoids, the hardware is only the starting point. You also need space, operators, maintenance, charging, spare parts, and a system for storing and checking the data. Downtime matters, too: ten thousand robots on paper doesn’t mean ten thousand robots collecting usable data continuously.

So I’d be cautious about giving a total without knowing the robot price and the collection setup. The more meaningful metric is cost per hour of useful data—or per successful demonstration. If the robots need frequent intervention or produce repetitive, low-quality data, scaling up just makes that inefficiency more expensive. I’d first validate the collection process with a smaller fleet, then scale once the data quality and utilization justify it.
